did.abstract: Correspondence, writings, and biographical material document the life and work of missionaries Frank J. Rawlinson and his wife Florence Lang Rawlinson. The Rawlinsons were based in Shanghai where Frank was editor of the Chinese Recorder from 1913 to 1937 and Florence was involved in distribution of handwork created by Chinese women in association with missions in China.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Frank Joseph Rawlinson was born in England in 1871 and came to the U.S. with his family in 1889. He graduated from Bucknell University in 1899 and married Carrie Mae Dietz, whom he had met at the Southern Baptist church he attended. Rawlinson, with his wife and first son, arrived in China in 1902 and initially served the Central China Mission of the Southern Baptist Convention. After serving as assistant editor for two years, Rawlinson was appointed editor in chief of the Chinese Recorder in 1913 and held that post until his death in 1937. While the family was on furlough in the U.S. in 1917, Carrie Mae Dietz died of a sudden illness, leaving Rawlinson with six children. In July 1917 Rawlinson married Florence Lang whom he had met on the ship to the U.S. as he was returning from China and Florence returning on furlough from her work with the YWCA in India.

After Frank received an M.A. from Teachers College, Columbia University, the Rawlinsons returned to China and Frank lectured at the Nanking University School for Missionaries and at the North China Union Language School in Beijing. As he read more widely in the Chinese classics and Buddhist texts, Rawlinson became opposed to missionary dogmatism and was a leader in the more liberal approach to appreciation of Chinese thought and culture. Under Rawlinson, the Chinese Recorder became a forum for debate on theological questions and the political claims of Chinese nationalism. In 1921 Rawlinson was dismissed by the Southern Baptist Mission Board because of his liberal views and interdenominational work, but he was quickly accepted as a missionary of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions and continued his work, including as organizer of the National Christian Conference held in Shanghai in 1922.

While on furlough in the U.S. 1925-1926, Rawlinson studied and lectured as a McFadden Mission Fellow at Union Theological Seminary in New York. Returning to China where Chinese politics had become increasingly nationalistic and anti-Christian, Rawlinson published Chinese Ideas of the Supreme Being (1926) and Naturalization of Christianity in China (1927), which sought to separate Christianity from imperialist domination or capitalist exploitation.

Rawlinson died on August 14, 1937 when a Chinese fighter plane that had been damaged by Japanese anti-aircraft fire accidently dropped a bomb on Shanghai, killing more than 1,500 people. At the time of his death Life magazine included photos of Rawlinson and his wife and called him "one of the most influential white men in China," commenting that Rawlinson "felt China could take Christianity without ceasing to be Chinese." Rawlinson's ashes were buried in the Pahsienjao Cemetery in Old Shanghai.

Florence Bodley Lang was born in 1883 in Toledo, Ohio. She went to Mumbai, India in 1915 where she served in administrative positions for the YWCA. Having met the Rawlinson family on the boat returning to the U.S. for furlough in 1916, Florence renewed her friendship with Frank Rawlinson when they were both in New York and they were married following the death of Frank's first wife in 1917. Florence became stepmother to Frank's six children and had three children of her own with him: Ruth, Jean, and John. In addition to overseeing the family household in Shanghai, Florence served as manager of the Industrial Mission Center, a store for distributing Chinese goods and was again in Shanghai for Anking Cross Stitch, which distributed cross stitch and handiwork done by women employed at various missions across China.
After her husband's death in 1937 Florence returned to the United States and lived primarily in Hartford, Connecticut where she died in 1961.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The collection is organized into three series: I. Correspondence; II. Writings; III Biographical material

accessrestrict.head: Conditions Governing Access
accessrestrict.p: The material is open for research.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Extensive substantial correspondence from Frank and Florence Rawlinson to family members in Series I provides insight into their life and work as influential missionaries in China. Frank's letters to his wife Florence during periods when they were separated and his letters to his children provide good documentation of his activities, concerns, and personality. Letters of Florence to her parents dating from 1915 to 1934 document her activities and relationships first in Mumbai, India where she was doing YWCA work and later from Shanghai where she oversaw the Rawlinson household and children as well as working as manager of a store that gathered, sold, and distributed Chinese handiwork in support of mission work with Chinese women. Letters from Florence to her stepchildren and children are detailed and informative about her activities and the daily concerns of the Rawlinson family.

In Series II, poems by Frank Rawlinson reveal his creative, insightful character while a selection of more scholarly works gives a glimpse of his work to understand the intersection between the Christian faith and Chinese culture. Rawlinson's writings and editorial work for the The Chinese Recorder sought to set a path for a non-imperialist introduction of Christianity to China. In the Preface to John Lang Rawlinson's biography of his father, historian John King Fairbank wrote that "Frank Rawlinson as editor of The Chinese Recorder had pursued a long struggle to lead Christianity in China into the modern day of nationalism and equal rights." A full bibliography of Rawlinson's writings is available in the biography written by his son.

The extensive typescript biography of Rawlinson by John Lang Rawlinson in Series III was published in 1990 as Rawlinson, the Recorder and China's Revolution : a topical biography of Frank Joseph Rawlinson, 1871-1937 by Cross Cultural Publications, Inc., Notre Dame, Indiana.
